extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and psychology (scholars interested in empiricism, pragmatism, and the philosophy of experience)
extracted.subtask_description: An expository/argumentative essay defending radical empiricism and pragmatism about the reality of relations and the function of concepts versus immediate experience. It addresses metaphysical and epistemological criteria for what counts as 'real', 'true', and philosophically successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of a philosophy's human success
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection with which any philosophy restores the fluent, instinctive world of life (redeeming innocence) is the measure of its human success and importance in philosophical history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophies differ in how they handle the dialectic that fragments immediate experience; those that most successfully restore the flowing sense of life and replace dialectical disjunctions with a redeemed unity are judged more successful. (Context: James contrasts approaches that ignore, resist, or negate dialectic to restore immediacy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional test for concepts (practical vs theoretic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether concepts serve primarily a practical role (orienting action, producing 'maps' for dealing with experience) or a theoretic role (yielding absolute understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson's claim that concepts have a practical but not a theoretical use is examined: concepts can orient us toward sensible flux and aid action, but they produce only static relations and maps, failing to penetrate the inner life of activity and history. Evaluation should note both practical indispensability and theoretic limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of conceptual knowledge (arrangement vs dynamic reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual knowledge is limited to arranging and comparing elements (static relations); it cannot by itself reveal the dynamic, causal, temporal life of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a conceptual system, ask whether it merely supplies eternal comparisons or coordinates (positions) or whether it also explains the inner, dynamic 'what-happens' character of experience. James argues that concepts give 'maps' (positions) but not the moving life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value-creation by concepts as non-theoretic achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts may create new values (motivation, feelings of power, sublimity) that change action, but this value-creating function is more connected to the active/practical life than to purely theoretic insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate conceptual systems for their capacity to change life and motivate action; such effects may be significant but are not equivalent to providing deeper theoretical penetration into the inner nature of the objects named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatist truth-criterion (re-insertion into experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts and universals are true only insofar as they lead us successfully back into sensible, particular experience; truth is tested by practical confluence with experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate truth claims under pragmatism, examine whether the intellectual operations 'dip back' into the finite stream of feeling and cohere with particular experiences. If abstract conclusions fail to reinsert into experience, they are practically deficient and thus pragmatically false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical empiricism about relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctive relations (the immediate relations between elements of experience) are as real as the terms related; relations are indefeasible parts of experience rather than mere verbal or conceptual add-ons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should treat experienced relations (continuity, contiguity, simultaneity, likeness, in-ness, on-ness, etc.) as ontologically significant components of the factual flux and not dismiss them as illusory or merely linguistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to conflating language with ontology
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not infer ontological doubleness or fragmentation of experience merely from the fact that language names a term multiple times in describing different relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the fallacy of composition that projects the multiplicity of phrases onto the multiplicity of the experienced thing; evaluate claims about 'two M's' critically—words can be plural while the experienced M remains one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility requirement for relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations must be intelligible in how they affect or make a difference to their terms; if a relation is said to be purely external and makes no difference to the terms, that claim appears irrational or unintelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing philosophical accounts of relations, require an account of how relations can be 'of' terms without altering them; demand coherence about whether relations are adventitious or internal to the nature of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of relations: intimate (internal) vs external
rubrics_metrics.description: Some relations are intimate and enter into the natures of the terms (e.g., similarity), while others (e.g., spatial where/when) are external and adventitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ontology and epistemology should distinguish relations that are intrinsic to the terms' identities from those that supervene contingently; this classification affects whether one tends toward pluralism or toward claims of absolute unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand that intellect reinsert conclusions into particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual operations ought to reinsert themselves with their conclusions into particular points of the immediate stream of life; if the intellect stays aloft among abstracts without such re-insertion, it fails its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophical systems by whether their abstractions have practical bearings on lived particulars—successful intellect both arranges and returns to sensible particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding logical/phenomenal category confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not slip from logical (language, concepts) into phenomenal (experience) points of view when arguing about reality; conflating the two creates fallacies in metaphysical claims about relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully separate claims about the structure of our descriptions from claims about the structure of the things described; critique arguments that substitute what is true of words for what is true of their referents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concatenated vs total-conflux union as ontological options
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish concatenated union (parts connected by paths of conjunctive transition, allowing partial conflux) from 'through-and-through' total-conflux (monistic each-in-all union); radical empiricism favors recognizing various concatenated relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging metaphysical accounts of unity, consider whether they account for the observed varieties of conflux (confluence, contiguity, likeness, nearness, simultaneousness) rather than enforcing an absolute monistic unity that denies such experienced relations.
